issue_context.title: Option to error on `module` namespaces
issue_context.body:
### Describe the feature

This feature request is motivated by Node's TypeScript integration. See https://github.com/nodejs/amaro/issues/168 for the backstory.

The request is for SWC to introduce a TypeScript-specific option (example:  `no_module_keyword_for_ts_namespace`) to error when the source text includes any form of namespace using the legacy `module` keyword:

- `module Foo {}`
- `declare module Foo {}`

This applies to both the ambient and non-ambient forms.  And applies to both instantiated and uninstantiated forms.

### Babel plugin or link to the feature description

https://github.com/nodejs/amaro/issues/168

### Additional context

### Exclusions

_Ambient module declarations_ (`declare module "specifier" {}`) are fine and should continue to be erased and not error.

### Amaro Usage

The initial user of this feature will be Amaro in Node.  Node needs to be able to show a helpful message to the user.  The returned error should identify this specific error so that we can display a human-readable message such as:

>`module` keyword is not supported. Use `namespace` instead.

review_comments: Is this really worth it? I'm asking because visitors have problems with the performance and the binary size.
Feel free to resolve this if you think it's too complex to merge the visitor logic of `ErrorOnTsModule` into the original visitor
Let me give this a try.

Currently, our TsStrip only visits top-level namespaces/modules and skips nested ones, while our ErrorOnTsModule visits both top-level and nested namespaces/modules and skips all other structures.

These behaviors are contradictory.

I attempted to wrap both in an external Visitor that encapsulates TsStrip and ErrorOnTsModule and switches state when entering or leaving a namespace. However, this approach would require proxying all methods of TsStrip and ErrorOnTsModule—TsStrip alone has 46 visitor methods that need to be proxied. This adds considerable complexity and increases the potential for errors.
Give up trying and leave things as they are.
We need to take a systematic approach to addressing this issue in #9984.
